document.title: DCI Report: The Rise of UBL and Al-Qa'ida and the Intelligence Community Response (Draft)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
document.note: Detailed summary of CIA efforts to apprehend bin Laden, 1989-2004. Covers his evolution from terrorist financier to major threat, Predator debates, FBI information-system critiques, and Afghan tribal leaders and Masood's role in capture attempts. "DIF" marks Denied in Full pages.

events.description: Bin Ladin joined the Afghan resistance almost immediately after the Soviet invasion.
Bin Ladin returned to Saudi Arabia to work in the family construction business after the Soviet withdrawal.
Bin Ladin resided in Sudan from 1991 to 1996, combining business with jihad.
Islamic extremists bombed a hotel housing US servicemen in Aden; Bin Ladin reportedly financed the group.
CTC established an Issue Station to focus on Bin Ladin as Sudan-based terrorist financier.
Saudi Arabia revoked Bin Ladin's citizenship (partly illegible).
CTC established an Issue Station to focus on Sudan-based financier Usama Bin Ladin.
Assassination attempt on Egyptian President Mubarak during visit to Ethiopia, to which Bin Ladin was connected.
Khobar Towers bombing in Saudi Arabia, which Bin Ladin said began the war between Muslims and the United States.
Interview with Bin Ladin in Afghanistan published in The Independent.
Bin Ladin left Sudan and relocated himself and his network to Afghanistan.
Terrorists prepared a casing study of the US Embassy in Nairobi.
Terrorists prepared a casing study of the US Embassy in Nairobi, five years before the attack.
The US indicted Bin Ladin for his call for a worldwide holy war against US citizens; the Taliban refused to cooperate in efforts to extradite him.
In spring 1999 a strategy review produced a comprehensive operational plan of attack against Bin Ladin and al-Qa'ida targets inside and outside Afghanistan.
Bombings of US embassies in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam, attributed to Bin Ladin's planning and execution.
US cruise missile attacks on targets in Sudan and Afghanistan (camps near Khowst); approx. 80 terrorists killed or injured; Bin Ladin escaped, possibly by hours.
US military increasingly interested in tribal Afghan sources reporting on Bin Ladin's movements for a possible cruise missile attack, while expressing concern over source reliability.
Plot to hijack a plane on the US east coast to free the 'blind sheikh' from prison, which CIA and FBI worked on together.
CIA Inspector General report on CTC concluded many CIA-FBI improvements had been institutionalized while noting persistent tensions.
Analysts' warnings that al-Qa'ida continued to view the US homeland as a high-priority target.
US cruise missile attacks on targets in Sudan and Afghanistan after the embassy bombings; Bin Ladin escaped, camps near Khowst targeted, about 80 terrorists reportedly injured or present.
Bombings of US embassies in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam, two weeks before the cruise missile strikes.
Military intelligence planning of a possible strike on Bin Laden focused on hunting camps used by UAE.
Military contemplated a cruise missile strike against Bin Ladin in Qandahar area; policy officials did not authorize it due to concerns about building identification and collateral damage.
CIA created a unit for strategic analytic work on al-Qa'ida (partly illegible).
Operational proposals for using a friendly tribal group to capture Bin Ladin discussed with the White House.
Plan to use friendly tribal group to capture Bin Ladin approved by the President in the form of the August 1998 MON.
Afghan tribal assets initiated a search and rendition operation in their area of influence.
MON authorized lethal force in offensive operations designed to capture Bin Ladin; Afghan group told lethal force only in the context of capture.
Reported ambush on a convoy in which UBL was a passenger; unsuccessful and unconfirmed; terminated when attackers heard women and children.
CIA began to put in place the elements of its operational strategy, 'The Plan'.
CIA learned Khalid al-Mihdhar's true name by early January 2000.
CIA learned Nawaf al-Hazmi's true name by early March 2000.
CIA sent cable to State, FBI, INS requesting al-Hazmi and al-Mihdhar be watch listed and denied entry to US.
During Ramadan 2000, CIA operations broke up terrorist cells planning attacks in the Persian Gulf region.
SEIB article 'Terrorism: Bin Ladin Threats Are Real'.
SEIB article 'Bin Ladin Determined to Strike in US'.
NSC Counterterrorism Coordinator asks CIA and DoD for new ideas against terrorists in Afghanistan, originating UAV idea.
CIA decides to recommend to NSC that the Predator program proceed with testing and operations.
First Predator reconnaissance mission over Afghanistan; Taliban unsuccessfully scrambled a MiG-21 during a flight.
In fall 2000 the Predator twice observed an individual most likely to be Bin Ladin.
DCI memo declaring war on Bin Ladin to CIA leaders.
During week of July 2, 2001 DCI phoned about 13 foreign liaison counterparts to urge redoubled efforts against al-Qa'ida.
Millennium threat: worldwide disruption effort led to arrests and breakup of cells.
Bin Ladin departs Sudan for Afghanistan.
The 19 hijackers of September 11 are said to have moved freely in the US and used the international banking system to transfer funds.
CIA operational proposals to capture Bin Ladin using a friendly tribal group discussed with the White House.
President approved the August 1998 MON authorizing use of the friendly tribal group to capture Bin Ladin after the East Africa bombings.
Afghan tribal assets began a search and rendition operation for UBL.
A MON for the first time authorized use of lethal force in operations designed to capture Bin Ladin.
Ambush reportedly launched against a convoy carrying UBL, terminated when attackers heard women and children; unconfirmed.
CIA began putting 'The Plan' in place in spring 1999, expanding CTC staffing and training.
Khalid al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi came to CIA attention in the Millennium period, leading to the Kuala Lumpur meeting.
National Security Advisor Dr. Rice remarked early in 2002 that the 9/11 attacks underscored that sound foreign policy begins at home.
CIA Inspector General report on CTC concludes that many improvements had been made and that CIA-FBI relationships had been institutionalized, while noting persistent tension between the two agencies.
CIA and FBI worked closely and successfully together to disrupt millennium plots and several other cases.

US cruise missile attacks on targets in Sudan and Afghanistan in response to the Nairobi and Dar es Salaam embassy bombings; Bin Ladin escaped injury. The OCR is garbled and the camps are said to be near Khowst, with about 80 terrorists reportedly targeted.
Tribal Afghan sources reported on Bin Ladin's movements, and the US military became interested in them for a possible cruise missile attack.
Military intelligence planning for a strike on Bin Ladin in Feb-Mar 1999 focused on a hunting camp used by UAE royals. UBL was reported at Shaykh Ali's Camp.

The military contemplated a cruise missile strike against Bin Ladin in the Qandahar area after tracking his whereabouts for almost a week. Policy officials did not authorize it because of concerns about building identification and collateral damage.
September 11 attacks by al-Qa'ida galvanized the US Government and foreign governments and prompted a military campaign in Afghanistan.
Embassy bombings in East Africa cited as an attack for which tactical warning was lacking.
USS Cole bombing cited as an attack for which tactical warning was lacking.
Millennium: IC launched a massive worldwide effort leading to arrests of many terrorists and breakup of overseas cells; no attacks occurred.
With an increase in Ramadan-related threat reporting in November-December 2000, CIA worked with partners to detect and preempt attacks.
In spring and summer 2001, CIA launched another massive disruption effort that stopped several attacks and caused others to be postponed.
USA Patriot Act of 2001 removed legal impediments to law enforcement sharing information with CIA.
Early years period of Bin Ladin as 'terrorist financier', as framed in the report's table of contents and section heading.
Bin Ladin gains prominence during the Afghan war by financing recruitment, transport and training of Arab volunteers who fought alongside the Afghan mujahedin against the Soviets.
Date of the draft DCI Report 'The Rise of UBL and Al-Qa'ida and the Intelligence Community Response'.
US cruise missile attack on al-Qa'ida training complex in northeastern Afghanistan, supported by integrated intelligence collection.
SEIB article 'Terrorism: Bin Ladin Threats Are Real' concluded threat indications were not disinformation.
SEIB article 'Bin Ladin Plans High Profile Attacks' said al-Qa'ida operatives expected dramatic consequences from next attacks.
SEIB article noted one Bin Ladin attack was delayed but preparations for other near-term attacks continued.
SEIB article 'Bin Ladin Determined to Strike in US' underscored his desire to attack the US homeland.
MON first authorized lethal force in offensive operations to capture Bin Ladin.
CIA established a unit to let analysts focus on strategic al-Qa'ida analysis.
Report on a plot to hijack a plane on the US east coast to free the 'blind sheikh' from prison. CIA and FBI worked together on the threat.

The Counterterrorist Center was established in 1986 per the original; this chunk's text refers to the Center's establishment in the 1980s and its later representation by more than a dozen agencies by 2001.
The Issue Station was established within the DCI Counterterrorist Center to focus on Bin Ladin, then the Sudan-based financier.
Assassination attempt on President Mubarak during a visit to Ethiopia; the report discusses Bin Ladin's connection to it.

In spring 1999, in response to the DCI's request, a review of operational strategy against Bin Ladin and a new strategic plan were produced. They set out a comprehensive operational plan of attack against the Bin Ladin al-Qa'ida target inside and outside Afghanistan, emphasizing the capture and rendering to justice of Bin Ladin and his principal lieutenants.
A further strategy element emerged in 2000 and 2001. The need for aggressive efforts to disrupt planned Bin Ladin-related terrorist operations worldwide diluted the focus on Bin Ladin himself.
By 2001 the Counterterrorist Center had representatives from more than a dozen agencies involved in the fight against terrorism.
Bin Ladin leaves Sudan and relocates himself and his network to Afghanistan.
Khobar Towers bombing in Saudi Arabia killing Americans, later cited by Bin Ladin.
The Independent publishes Bin Ladin's interview from Afghanistan declaring war against the US.
al-Qa'ida issues a fatwa under the World Islamic Front banner declaring a duty to kill Americans and allies.
Terrorists prepare casing study of the US Embassy in Nairobi, five years before the 1998 attack.
Al-Qa'ida terrorists prepared a casing study of the US Embassy in Nairobi, five years before the attack.
East Africa embassy attacks, including the US Embassy in Nairobi, which al-Qa'ida had cased in 1993.
The US indicted Bin Ladin for his call for a worldwide holy war against US citizens. The Taliban then refused to extradite him.
Bin Ladin joined the Afghan resistance following the Soviet invasion.
Bin Ladin press interview claiming mortar shell that failed to explode was a sign from God.
Bin Ladin returned to Saudi Arabia after Soviet withdrawal.
Bin Ladin began residence in Sudan (1991-1996).
Islamic extremists bombed a hotel housing US servicemen in Aden; Bin Ladin financed the group.
CIA established Issue Station within the DCI Counterterrorist Center to focus on Bin Ladin.
CIA learned Nawaf al-Hazmi's true name by early March 2000, first opportunity to watch list him.
CIA knew Khalid al-Mihdhar's true name by early January 2000, first watch-list opportunity.
CIA linked a USS Cole bombing suspect to the Kuala Lumpur meeting, another missed watch-list opportunity.
CIA asked State, FBI, INS and others to watch list al-Hazmi and al-Mihdhar and deny entry to the US.
Kuala Lumpur meeting in which al-Mihdhar and al-Hazmi participated.
During Ramadan autumn 2000, CIA and partners broke up terrorist cells planning attacks on US and foreign targets in the Persian Gulf region.
Idea of UAV reconnaissance in Afghanistan originated after NSC request.
Decision made in late May 2000 to recommend to NSC that the Predator program proceed with testing and operations.
First Predator reconnaissance mission over Afghanistan.
Predator twice observed an individual most likely Bin Ladin but no means to react.
In fall 2000 the Predator twice observed an individual most likely Bin Ladin, but there was no means to react.
CIA was authorized to deploy the Predator for reconnaissance purposes following policy discussions.
During the Millennium threat in late 1999, CIA told the President to expect 5 to 15 terrorist attacks against American interests.
DCI testimony to Congress that Bin Ladin is planning attacks and will strike anywhere.
DCI sent a memo to CIA leaders declaring war on Bin Ladin and demanding no resources be spared.
During week of July 2, 2001 the DCI phoned about 13 foreign liaison counterparts urging redoubled efforts against al-Qa'ida; CTC chief and Near East Division chief made further calls.
UBL departed Sudan; CIA then targeted his Afghanistan presence.
By spring 1998 CIA opened contact with Northern Alliance Commander Masood.

key_claims: Bin Ladin gained prominence during the Afghan war by financing recruitment, transport and training of Arab fighters.
Al-Qa'ida (Islamic Salvation Foundation) was organized with family wealth and Gulf donations and ran guesthouses and camps in Pakistan and Afghanistan.
Many future al-Qa'ida leaders met and fought alongside Bin Ladin in Afghanistan.
In Sudan from 1991 to 1996 Bin Ladin combined business and jihad and financed extremists.
In the early 1990s CIA assessed Bin Ladin mainly as a terrorist financier, not the head of an organization targeting the US.
CTC created an Issue Station in January 1996 to focus on Bin Ladin.
Through the early 1990s CIA saw Bin Ladin mainly as a financier of other terrorist groups, not head of a separate network targeting the US.
Bin Ladin relocated his network from Sudan to Afghanistan in 1996, where Taliban sanctuary let it grow into a strategic threat.
Al-Qa'ida attack preparation involved patient, meticulous planning, such as the 1993 casing study for the Nairobi embassy.
Al-Qa'ida showed interest in chemical and biological weapons, calling acquisition a religious duty.
Al-Qa'ida's plotting, planning, recruiting and training in the late 1990s would not have been possible without Taliban-sanctioned sanctuary in Afghanistan.
The Taliban aided Bin Ladin, provided terrorist camps and refused to cooperate in extraditing him after his 1998 US indictment.
Afghanistan, with its vast infrastructure of camps and facilities, gave Bin Ladin an isolated and relatively safe environment from which to oversee worldwide terrorist activities.
Militants who trained in Afghanistan were sent to fight jihads in places such as Kashmir.

Al-Qa'ida operations involved careful, patient and meticulous preparation, including extensive surveillance and casing studies, such as the 1993 Nairobi embassy study made five years before the attack.
Al-Qa'ida was interested in acquiring chemical and biological weapons and described this as a religious duty.
Bin Ladin stressed indoctrination and extremist religious ideas, arguing that the regimes of Muslim countries are not true believers and should be overthrown as a religious duty.
CIA counterterrorism cooperation with the FBI improved from 1995 onward but remained limited by differences in mission, culture and tradecraft.
The 20 Aug 1998 cruise missile strikes responded to evidence of Bin Ladin's responsibility for the Nairobi and Dar es Salaam embassy bombings.
Intelligence suggested Bin Ladin was at camps near Khowst, but he escaped, possibly by hours.
Demands for multiple corroborating sources and concern about civilian collateral damage constrained approval for further strikes on Bin Ladin.
The military was concerned about the reliability of tribal Afghan sources for locating Bin Ladin.
By Aug 2001 analysts judged that al-Qa'ida still viewed the US homeland as a high-priority target.
Policy demand for corroborated, time-and-place-specific intelligence on Bin Ladin, plus collateral-damage concerns, constrained cruise missile strike authorization.
The Aug 1998 strikes targeted camps near Khowst but Bin Ladin escaped.
In May 1999 a strike on Bin Ladin in the Qandahar area was not authorized due to building identification and collateral damage concerns.
CIA personnel and budget cuts in the 1990s limited its ability to shift resources to counterterrorism.
CIA identified al-Qa'ida's growing interest in cash couriers and hawala networks in the Middle East and South Asia.
CIA assessed that none of the available capture units had more than a ten percent chance of capturing Bin Ladin.
The Afghan tribal group operating from September 1998 never produced significant results, and a reported 9 Aug 2000 ambush could not be confirmed.
Lack of timely, accurate intelligence on UBL's plans, intentions and travel and heavy security hindered capture operations.
CIA actions against al-Qa'ida led it to increase security and compartmentation, making future plots harder to uncover.
CIA identified al-Mihdhar and al-Hazmi around the Kuala Lumpur meeting but missed chances to watch list them until August 2001.
Analysts warned in summer 2001 that Bin Ladin threats were real.
CIA judged capture options against Bin Ladin in Afghanistan had less than ten percent chance of success.
By late 1999 CIA concluded tribal assets, Masood, and liaison services were extremely poor options, prompting the Predator initiative.
The Predator's first Afghan mission flew September 7, 2000, and twice in fall 2000 it observed a probable Bin Ladin.
Al-Qa'ida's security and Afghan sanctuary prevented tactical warning of the embassy bombings, USS Cole and 9/11.
CIA declared war on Bin Ladin in a December 4, 1998 DCI memo.
The report says the war on terrorism will be long and difficult and will need sustained multi-year resources to recapitalize the intelligence infrastructure.
The report judges that another major terrorist attack is not just possible but likely despite efforts.
The report says the 9/11 hijackers moved freely in the US and used the international banking system to transfer funds, so the war must also be pursued at home.
The report says successes against the al-Qa'ida leadership and worldwide cells have disrupted its command and control, but it retains the capacity to mount destructive attacks.
The report calls for closer sharing of information between intelligence and law enforcement agencies and for countries that previously ignored terrorism to choose sides.
